title: Toddlers Comforting Their Mothers
text:
When does concern for others first appear in children? At the National Institute of Mental Health in the United States, Carolyn Zahn-Waxler, Marian Radke-Yarrow and their colleagues studied this question in the setting where it matters most: the home.

They followed children through the second year of life, starting at around thirteen to fifteen months. The mothers were trained to observe and record what happened whenever someone near their child was hurt, sad or upset, whether the child had caused it or simply witnessed it. In addition, researchers visited the homes, and from time to time the mother or the visitor would pretend to be in distress, for example bumping a knee and saying "ouch," or acting sad.

In the early months, children often just watched, or became upset themselves. Over the following year, their responses changed markedly. More and more often, they patted or hugged the person in distress, brought them a toy or a blanket, said kind words, or tried to fix the problem. They also showed signs of trying to understand what was wrong, looking back and forth between the person and the cause of the pain.

By their second birthday, many children were showing clear, if simple, empathy and comfort toward others.
lesson: Empathy begins very early and grows through daily life at home. When a toddler pats your arm after you get hurt, notice it and welcome it.
people: Carolyn Zahn-Waxler, Marian Radke-Yarrow and colleagues
location: National Institute of Mental Health, Bethesda, USA
source: Zahn-Waxler, C., Radke-Yarrow, M., Wagner, E., and Chapman, M. (1992). Development of concern for others. Developmental Psychology, 28(1), 126-136.
